uncited: Multi-view projection voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a voxel grid by rasterizing the geometry from multiple camera viewpoints, typically aligned with the principal axes of the scene's bounding box.
This approach solves the coverage gaps and geometric distortions inherent in single-view projection methods, which fail when surface normals are perpendicular to the view direction.
It differs from single-view methods by ensuring comprehensive coverage through redundancy, and from compute-shader-based methods by leveraging standard graphics pipeline rasterization.

The family relies on the principle that projecting a 3D object from multiple orthogonal directions ensures that every surface element is visible from at least one viewpoint, preventing "shadow" voxels caused by occlusion or grazing angles.
**View Direction Selection:** Cameras are positioned along the principal axes (X, Y, Z) of the scene's bounding box.
The view direction is parallel to the axis being projected onto.

**Orthographic Projection:** Orthographic cameras are used to map 3D world coordinates directly to 2D screen coordinates without perspective distortion, simplifying the mapping from pixel coordinates to voxel grid indices.
**Fragment-to-Voxel Mapping:** Rasterized fragments are transformed from clip space to voxel grid space.
The mapping uses the scene's bounding box and target resolution to determine the integer voxel coordinates $(i, j, k)$.
**Atomic Writes or Synthesis:** To handle concurrent writes from multiple triangles or views, atomic operations are used when writing directly to a 3D texture.
Alternatively, intermediate 2D buffers (sheets) are synthesized into a final 3D representation.
**Degeneracy Handling:** Triangles parallel to a view direction may project to a line or point.
These cases are handled by either skipping the view for that triangle, expanding the triangle, or rasterizing along a different axis where the projection area is non-zero.
Multi-view projection voxelization is a foundational technique in computer graphics for converting polygonal meshes into volumetric representations suitable for ray marching or ray tracing.
Its origins lie in early volume rendering and voxelization algorithms that sought to overcome the limitations of single-view rasterization, such as self-occlusion and aliasing.
The use of three orthogonal views (X, Y, Z) became a standard heuristic to ensure manifold integrity and 6-connectivity in the resulting voxel grid.
Modern implementations often integrate this with GPU compute shaders or specialized hardware rasterization pipelines to achieve real-time performance.
The technique is widely used in global illumination, collision detection, and neural radiance field (NeRF) preprocessing.
